Ironically, the Blue Wave Could Make Hyperscalers "Good Businesses Again" by Forcing Capex Discipline ©@Bianca Constantinescu's Images via Canva, @Angelo Dee from ภาพของSakorn Sukkasemsakorn via Canva
Key Takeaways

Democrats won control of the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterms, and state results point to more limits on building data centers but fewer outright bans.

Tighter rules that slow the build-out would help Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft shareholders, because less capex while capacity stays scarce repairs free cash flow without hurting demand.

Free cash flow needs the repair: Amazon's was a $34.8 billion outflow in the September quarter, and Meta's turned negative.

The companies still set their own budgets, and Alphabet's capex keeps climbing, so the 2027 spending plans due early next year are what to watch.

Democrats won the House and the Senate on Tuesday, and one investor thinks that could be the best news in a while for shareholders of Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ), Alphabet (GOOG), Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) and Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ).

That sounds backward. Tighter rules on data centers should mean a slower AI build-out, and AI stocks have been priced for a faster one.

But the investor who posts as BuccoCapital on X thinks the slowdown is good for them: "Dem sweep is bullish AI because everyone spends less on capex and diffusion has time to catch up to the buildout. Labs can't miss on revenue bc they are compute constrained."

Another user pushed back that the market's earnings growth leans on chipmakers like Nvidia and Micron, and he waved that off. On the big cloud spenders, he wrote: "The hypers would be good businesses again."

Ironically, I think he's right.

Incumbents get the edge

Jim Cramer, host of CNBC's Mad Money, went through the state-by-state results on data centers and found "more restrictions being put on building them but fewer outright bans." He thinks that "would seem to favor incumbents PLUS spending within means as opposed to endless buildouts."

That's the setup the four giants should want. They already run the capacity, and new rules make everyone's next site slower to build, theirs included. With capacity that tight, demand holds up: Amazon's management says the capacity it adds is sold as soon as it's installed.

And the market already rewards restraint. On Monday's Mad Money, Cramer pointed out that "the only hyperscalers that did dial back its CapEx plans, Microsoft, saw the best reaction from the market for doing so." (Its stock still fell, he added, just by less than the rest.)

The Nasdaq-100, which is the 100 largest non-financial stocks in the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC), is up 12.4% year-to-date (YTD) at the time of this writing. Here's why the Vanguard Morningstar Mega Cap Growth ETF (NYSEMKT: MGK) is an excellent low-cost way to buy the dip on top growth stocks.

Image source: Getty Images.
The Mega Cap Growth ETF has 67.6% in 10 stocks

The Mega Cap Growth ETF is essentially a more concentrated version of the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (NYSEMKT: VUG). The Mega Cap ETF has 52 holdings compared to 135 for the Growth ETF. The expense ratio of the Mega Cap ETF is 0.05% -- only slightly higher than the Growth ETF's 0.03% expense ratio. It's worth noting that 0.03% is the lowest you'll find for any ETF. Investing in leading Nasdaq and NYSE growth stocks

The Mega Cap Growth ETF is a great buy for investors who believe today's most valuable companies will continue leading the broader market over the long term. But some investors may lean toward buying a Nasdaq-100 index ETF, such as the popular Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ: QQQ), rather than the Mega Cap Growth ETF. The issue with that strategy is twofold.

For starters, the Invesco QQQ Trust has a relatively high expense ratio of 0.18%. And, more importantly, it invests exclusively in Nasdaq-listed non-financial companies -- meaning it excludes key growth stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).

AMD’s Data Center Sales Nearly Doubled, but Its Own Stock Rally Just Cost It $1.1 Billion

AMD's Data Center Sales Nearly Doubled, but Its Own Stock Rally Just Cost It $1.1 Billion © Kittipong Jirasukhanont from PhonlamaiPhoto's Images and Nickel_Bell from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

AMD beat third-quarter estimates as data center revenue climbed 97% to $8.5 billion, and it guided to about $17 billion of fourth-quarter revenue.

The results also included a $1.1 billion charge for the penny-a-share warrants AMD gave OpenAI and Meta, and that charge grows as AMD's stock rises and its chips ship.

The charge doesn't hit cash or adjusted earnings, but the dilution behind it is real, and free cash flow separately fell to about 4% of revenue as AMD built up inventory.

AMD trades at 42x forward earnings, above its three-year average, so NVIDIA's report later this month and AMD's own fourth quarter are the next tests.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) beat Wall Street's estimates after Tuesday's close, with data center sales nearly doubling.

But the quarter also brought the first bill for the stock AMD promised OpenAI and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ). Most of that bill comes from AMD's own rally.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on AMD, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See AMD's Analyst Ratings

What exactly happened

Here's the quarter against Bloomberg's consensus estimates:

Revenue: $13.38 billion, against $13.08 billion expected

Adjusted EPS: $2.09, against $1.97 expected

Data center revenue: $8.5 billion, up 97% from a year earlier and ahead of the $8.19 billion estimate

Fourth-quarter guidance: about $17 billion of revenue, plus or minus 3%

And CEO Lisa Su raised the stakes for next year on the call: "Based on our current visibility, we now expect revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027."

The GAAP results also included a $1.1 billion charge, or $0.66 a share, for the warrants AMD granted OpenAI and Meta. Last quarter, that line was zero.

Under the deals, each company can buy up to 160 million AMD shares at a penny apiece as it rolls out up to 6 gigawatts of AMD chips. The last batch unlocks only if AMD's stock reaches $600. AMD started booking the warrants once its MI450 chips began shipping. CFO Jean Hu said on the call that the charge mostly reflected "the increase in our share price and the changes in the estimated probability of meeting the warrant conditions." AMD's stock rose about 21% last quarter and closed it around $630, above that $600 line.

A bill that grows with the stock

The charge is also set to grow. Hu expects it "to increase as we and our customers progress under this agreement." So every rally and every chip shipment to these two customers adds to it.

title: Meta Goes to Europe for Debt After Raising $15 Billion
detail:
Meta Goes to Europe for Debt After Raising $15 Billion
Renato Neves, CFA
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 12:53 PM MST 1 min read
META
Trade META on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) launched its first euro-denominated bond sale on Wednesday, a day after raising $15 billion in the U.S. dollar market, Bloomberg reported. It is Meta's first bond sale outside its home market. Meta shares were up 1.65% as of 9:50 a.m. ET.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Sign with META.

Is META fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

META GF Value chart

The euro offering comes in six parts, with maturities from just over four years to more than 38 years. Initial pricing is around 140 basis points over mid-swaps for the shortest tranche and around 370 basis points for the longest. Citigroup and Morgan Stanley are managing the sale, which is expected to price later on Wednesday.

Meta priced Tuesday's dollar notes in five tranches maturing from 2031 to 2056, with coupons from 5.850% to 7.500%. Investors placed as much as $58 billion of bids for the deal, Bloomberg said. The coupons are higher than in Meta's April sale of $25 billion of notes, when its 2031 bonds paid 4.550% and its 2056 bonds 6.300%. The debt follows Meta's plans last week for equity offerings of around $97.5 billion to fund its AI build-out.

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) is borrowing $15 billionand the annual coupon bill comes to nearly $1 billion. The social media and AI company priced five bond tranches on November 3, with settlement scheduled for November 5. Shares rose 1.77% at 9.14 a.m. ET in November 4 premarket trading. For investors, the deal puts a hard number on the recurring financing burden alongside Meta's infrastructure spending.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Sign with META.

Is META fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

META GF Value chart

The borrowing stretches from 2031 to 2056. Meta's term sheet lists $3.25 billion carrying a 5.85% coupon, another $3.25 billion at 6.25%, and $4 billion at 6.55%. The two longest tranches add $1.75 billion at 7.35% and $2.75 billion at 7.5%. Multiply each tranche by its coupon and the annual cash interest totals $990.125 million, producing a weighted coupon of approximately 6.60%. That calculation measures annual coupon payments; accounting interest expense could differ.

Meta's GF Score of 99/100 shows considerable underlying strength, with profitability, growth and momentum reaching the outer edge of the radar chart. Financial strength and GF Value sit closer to the center, making borrowing capacity and valuation useful areas for closer scrutiny. The score supports the quality case, but future returns may increasingly depend on how much cash remains after capital expenditure, lease payments and interest. Strong operating growth could help absorb those demands; the key test is whether cash generation keeps pace with the spending commitments.

Tech stocks were mixed Wednesday afternoon, with the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) rising 0.5% and the State Street SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF (XSD) falling 2.5%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor index declined 3.1%.

In corporate news, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) issued a stronger-than-expected Q4 revenue outlook late Tuesday as Q3 results topped Wall Street estimates, driven by strength in its data center business. Shares eased 0.2%.

Meta (META), Amazon (AMZN), CoreWeave (CRWV) and other data center developers may face increased regulatory hurdles for planned AI projects following Democratic victories in several US gubernatorial races, most notably in Texas, which accounts for nearly 30% of US data center capacity and just elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who has pledged to halt new data center approvals until lawmakers establish additional protections for local communities, Bloomberg reported. Meta shares were up 2.9%, Amazon rose past 7%, and CoreWeave fell over 9%.

Datadog (DDOG) shares fell past 14% after the cloud monitoring and security platform issued a soft Q4 revenue forecast, signaling a growth deceleration despite Q3 results topping consensus estimates.

Oracle (ORCL) has axed a $7 billion chip-leasing contract with Tencent, yielding to pressure from the White House, the Financial Times reported. Oracle shares were down 0.9%.
